objects.name: Error
objects.description: Returned whenever a request fails.

fields.name: Code
fields.description: Machine-readable reason the request failed.

fields.name: Message

fields.name: RequestID

objects.name: Profile
objects.description: Somebody's public face, with pictures attached to it.

fields.name: ID
fields.description: Unique identifier for this row.

fields.name: TenantID
fields.description: Tenant this row belongs to. Every query is scoped by it.

fields.name: CreatedAt
fields.description: When this row was created. Set automatically and never changes.

fields.name: DisplayName
fields.description: What to call them.

fields.name: ProfileImageFileID
fields.description: The picture. A <role>_file_id column is the declaration: the role names the endpoints and the permission keys, and rig_file is the only table it could point at, so the naming rule exempts it.

fields.name: BannerFileID
fields.description: A second one on the same table, which is the reason the role is in the name at all. The rule's own suggestion, rig_file_id, allows exactly one.

objects.name: ProfileAttachment
objects.description: A gallery is a table. Many files against one row is a child table with one file column, not a second mechanism.

fields.name: ID
fields.description: Unique identifier for this row.

fields.name: TenantID
fields.description: Tenant this row belongs to. Every query is scoped by it.

fields.name: CreatedAt
fields.description: When this row was created. Set automatically and never changes.

fields.name: ProfileID
fields.description: Reached through a composite key carrying the tenant, which is the shape rig recommends wherever the target is tenant-scoped. Its index leads with the tenant, and that is the index the generated queries want.

fields.name: DocumentFileID
fields.description: The same shape, deliberately left without an index so the rule has something to say. Before the tenant-carrying form was denormalized onto its column, it had nothing to say about either of these.

fields.name: ThumbnailFileID
fields.description: The control. Named like a file column and pointing at profile instead, so it is not one — and it still gets the ordinary naming advice.

fields.name: Caption
fields.description: What the attachment is.

objects.name: ProfileAttachmentFilter
objects.description: Conditions a ProfileAttachment must satisfy to match a search.

fields.name: Equals
fields.description: Fields that must equal the given value.

fields.name: NotEquals
fields.description: Fields that must not equal the given value.

fields.name: GreaterThan
fields.description: Fields that must be greater than the given value.

fields.name: SmallerThan
fields.description: Fields that must be less than the given value.

fields.name: GreaterOrEqual
fields.description: Fields that must be greater than or equal to the given value.

fields.name: SmallerOrEqual
fields.description: Fields that must be less than or equal to the given value.

fields.name: Contains
fields.description: Fields that must be one of the given values.

fields.name: NotContains
fields.description: Fields that must not be one of the given values.

fields.name: Like
fields.description: Text fields that must match the given pattern.

fields.name: NotLike
fields.description: Text fields that must not match the given pattern.

fields.name: Null
fields.description: Fields that must be null.

fields.name: NotNull
fields.description: Fields that must not be null.

fields.name: OrCondition
fields.description: Combine this filter's conditions with OR instead of AND.

fields.name: NestedFilters
fields.description: Sub-filters combined with this one, so that AND and OR can be mixed to any depth.

fields.name: Without
fields.description:
Relations with no row matching the given conditions. An empty one asks for no related row at all.

This is where a negation belongs when what you mean is "not": it negates whether a matching related row exists, so a row with no related row at all satisfies it. The negative operators above negate the comparison instead and still require the related row to be there — "no related row called X" is here, "a related row not called X" is NotEquals.

objects.name: RigFile
objects.description: One uploaded file. Metadata only — the bytes live in the blob store, and the storage key never leaves the server.

fields.name: ID
fields.description: Unique identifier for this row.

fields.name: TenantID
fields.description: Tenant this row belongs to. Every query is scoped by it.

fields.name: StorageKey
fields.description: Where the bytes are, derived from the identifier and never from a name.

fields.name: URL
fields.description: Where the file is served from. It is a column so a synced row carries it and a client can render the file without asking anything first.

fields.name: FileName
fields.description: What the file was called when it arrived.

fields.name: ContentType
fields.description: What the bytes were sniffed to be, which is not what the client claimed.

fields.name: SizeBytes
fields.description: How large the object is.

fields.name: UploadedAt
fields.description: When the bytes landed. Null means the row was inserted and the upload has not finished, which is what makes an abandoned upload reapable.

fields.name: Without
fields.description:
Relations with no row matching the given conditions. An empty one asks for no related row at all.

This is where a negation belongs when what you mean is "not": it negates whether a matching related row exists, so a row with no related row at all satisfies it. The negative operators above negate the comparison instead and still require the related row to be there — "no related row called X" is here, "a related row not called X" is NotEquals.

endpoints.name: Restore
endpoints.description:
The deletion stamp is cleared and the row appears in reads again. It works for 30 days after the deletion; past that the row is no longer eligible and this answers 409.

Restoring a row that was never deleted is not an error. It is already in the state the caller asked for, and answering otherwise would make a retry of a request whose response went missing look like a failure.

The request carries no fields. What to do when the world has moved on while the row was retired — a unique value taken by something created since — is the application's decision, and it is made in the restore hook: refuse, or change the row so that it fits.

Every rule then runs against whatever the hook settled on, not only the ones for fields it touched. The row was not live, so nothing about it has been checked against the world it is returning to.
